title: "Component processing and labeling"

## The ticket

Wednesday, 6:40 a.m., shift handoff. Tuesday's donation — the one module 2 followed through
quarantine — cleared every test overnight and is sitting released in Lakeshore Blood Center's
processing lab: a bag of red cells, a bag of plasma, a bag of platelets, all still bulk
components without their final labels. That part is routine. What isn't routine is what the
overnight supervisor flags next.

Around 2:00 a.m., Lakeshore's Blood Establishment Computer Software (BECS — the system you've
seen do two jobs already: holding donor eligibility in module 1, gating quarantine release in
module 2) received a scheduled vendor update. Buried inside was a routine-looking content
refresh: the latest quarterly product code table published by ICCBBA (International Council for
Commonality in Blood Banking Automation — more on exactly who that is shortly), the organization
that governs the barcode standard printed on every unit Lakeshore ships. Nobody flagged the
timing for Quality's review — it looked like reference data, not a system change.

Between 2:00 and 6:15 a.m., roughly forty units — mostly leukoreduced red cells, plus a few
pooled cryoprecipitate units — finished processing and had their final labels printed. Every one
of those labels carries a product code that was correct at 1:59 a.m. and has been one revision
behind since 2:00. None of the forty units have shipped. They're sitting in inventory, correctly
typed, correctly separated, correctly modified — and, as of this morning, carrying barcodes that
no longer match what ICCBBA's current table says those codes mean.

Your Quality Analyst wants to know: are these units actually mislabeled? And if they are, what
has to happen before any of them is eligible to leave quarantine-adjacent status and enter
Lakeshore's real inventory? Answering that requires knowing what a blood component label
actually has to say, why it says it in a barcode instead of just words, and who gets to decide
what that barcode means.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

The physical product here is fine. The red cells are still red cells, still the right blood
type, still processed and stored correctly. What's actually at risk is whether the *label* —
the thing every downstream system and person trusts without re-verifying the product itself —
still accurately says what the product is. A hospital transfusion service scans a barcode and
trusts it. Lakeshore's own inventory system trusts it. If the code on the label no longer means
what the current, authoritative table says it means, that trust is now resting on stale data,
not a stale product — and the two are easy to confuse, because nothing about the bag looks
wrong.

You already have a name for this failure mode, just under a different label (no pun intended):
**configuration identity and naming standards.** Think about what happens when a CI naming or
tagging schema changes and gets pushed into a production CMDB integration without change control:
every CI tagged under the old schema isn't *wrong*, exactly, but it no longer describes itself the
way the current standard says it should, and anything downstream that trusts the tag inherits that
drift silently. Now raise the stakes: imagine that naming standard isn't yours to define. It's set
by an international registration authority, applied identically at every accredited blood
establishment on six continents, and an FDA investigator or AABB assessor can ask you,
specifically, to prove you're using the current version.

That's exactly what ISBT 128 is, and it's why this module exists: **ISBT 128 is what a CMDB
naming convention would look like if an international registration authority enforced it and
an inspector audited it.** And the second half of this morning's problem is a distinct but
related ITSM failure: pushing an updated product code table into a live, production
label-printing pipeline — mid-shift, with no advance review, no test run, no coordinated
timing with Quality — is a **change**, not a content edit. Treating it as the latter is how a
vendor's "routine data refresh" becomes forty units with a data-integrity gap nobody signed off
on creating.

## The rule, in plain English

A donation doesn't become inventory-ready the moment it clears quarantine. Five things have to
happen, roughly in this order, before a component is eligible for release:

1. **Separation.** A single whole blood donation gets spun and split into distinct components —
   typically red cells, plasma, and platelets, sometimes further processed into cryoprecipitate
   — each one a physically different product with a different clinical use and, critically, a
   different shelf life. (Apheresis, the machine-collection method module 2 mentioned in
   passing, produces a more targeted single component directly, but everything from here on
   applies the same way either way.)
2. **Modifications, where ordered or required.** A component may get one or more further
   treatments before it's finished: **leukoreduction** (filtering out white blood cells to
   reduce certain transfusion reactions), **irradiation** (treating the product to prevent a
   rare but serious reaction in vulnerable patients), **washing** (removing residual plasma
   proteins), or **pooling** (combining several donations' worth of a component — cryoprecipitate
   and some platelet products are commonly pooled — into a single unit). This lesson names these
   because they change what has to appear on the label; it doesn't teach when each one is
   clinically indicated — that's a transfusion-medicine decision, not a Director-level regulatory
   one.
3. **Expiration dating, specific to the exact component and modification.** This is not one
   clock. It's several, running in parallel from the same donation, and they can differ by orders
   of magnitude — you'll see the actual numbers in the next section.
4. **The container label**, carrying a defined set of required content, some of it human-readable
   text and some of it a machine-readable barcode.
5. **Release-eligibility.** A component isn't eligible for release into inventory until it
   carries a complete, correct label reflecting everything above — accurately, and against the
   *current* version of whatever table or standard the label's coded content depends on. This is
   where this module ends; what happens to a released, correctly labeled unit next — storage,
   shipping, distribution to a hospital — is module 4's job.

Lakeshore's forty units cleared steps 1 through 3 without incident. The problem sits entirely in
step 4, and it's specifically what makes step 5 — release-eligibility — genuinely uncertain
until someone checks.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.121(c)(1)–(4) | "Six-oh-six point one-two-one, paragraph c, sub-one through sub-four" | The container label must include the product's proper name, the manufacturer's identity and unique facility identifier, the donor/lot number, and the expiration date (with the hour, if the dating period is 72 hours or less). | The baseline human-readable content every one of Lakeshore's forty units already has correct — this isn't where the problem is. |
| 21 CFR 606.121(c)(9) | "Six-oh-six point one-two-one, paragraph c, sub-nine" | The ABO group and Rh type must be conspicuously designated on the label, using a defined format based on the Anti-D test result. | Also unaffected this morning — ABO/Rh typing doesn't depend on the product code table at all. |
| 21 CFR 606.121(c)(13) | "Six-oh-six point one-two-one, paragraph c, sub-thirteen" | The label must carry a machine-readable barcode, approved for use by FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER), containing at minimum: a unique facility identifier, the lot number relating to the donor, the product code, and ABO/Rh. | The exact requirement Lakeshore's forty units are now in question against — the product code inside that barcode is the piece that drifted. |
| 21 CFR 606.121(c)(8)(ii) | "Six-oh-six point one-two-one, paragraph c, sub-eight, clause ii" | A transfusion-intended product's label must carry the statement pointing to the Circular of Information (a separate reference document, not repeated on the label itself). | Brief context: the label doesn't have to say everything about the product — it has to say enough, and point to where the rest lives. |
| 21 CFR 610.53(b) | "Six-ten point five-three, paragraph b" | A table of fixed dating periods (maximum time a product can be stored before expiring), specific to each product type, storage temperature, and modification. | The regulatory reason Tuesday's red cells, plasma, and platelets are already running on three separate expiration clocks, not one. |

## The actual text

Start with the baseline content requirement, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.121.md`
(retrieved from eCFR):

> (c) The container label must include the following information, as well as other specialized
> information as required in this section for specific products:
>
> (1) The proper name of the product in a prominent position, with any appropriate modifiers and
> attributes.
>
> (2) The name, address, unique facility identifier, and, if a licensed product, the license
> number of each manufacturer...
>
> (3) The donor or lot number relating the unit to the donor...
>
> (4)(i) The expiration date, including the day, month, and year, and, if the dating period for
> the product is 72 hours or less, including any product prepared in a system that might
> compromise sterility, the hour of expiration.

Notice (4)(i) closely: most components get a day/month/year expiration, but anything with a
72-hour-or-shorter dating period — pooled platelets prepared in an open system are a common
example — has to carry an actual expiration *hour*, not just a date. That's not a formatting
preference; it's the regulation recognizing that some components age out fast enough that "today"
isn't precise enough.

Now the requirement actually in question this morning — the machine-readable barcode:

> (13) The container label of blood or blood components intended for transfusion must bear
> encoded information in a format that is machine-readable and approved for use by the Director,
> CBER.
>
> ...
>
> (iii) *What information must be machine-readable?* Each label must have machine-readable
> information that contains, at a minimum:
>
> (A) A unique facility identifier;
>
> (B) Lot number relating to the donor;
>
> (C) Product code; and
>
> (D) ABO and Rh of the donor...

Read that list carefully, because it's doing something worth noticing: **it never says "ISBT
128."** The regulation requires a machine-readable format approved by CBER, containing those
four specific elements. It doesn't name a standard. That distinction matters, and this lesson
comes back to it directly in the traps section below — for now, hold onto this: the *requirement*
for a scannable product code is regulation. The *specific standard* nearly every U.S. blood
establishment uses to satisfy it is something else entirely.

The Circular of Information reference, briefly — the label doesn't repeat clinical guidance, it
points to a separate document required to accompany the product:

> (ii) "See circular of information for indications, contraindications, cautions, and methods of
> infusion."

That's the whole label-side footprint of the Circular of Information for this lesson's purposes:
a required pointer statement, not required content on the label itself. The Circular is a
standard reference document about the product type that a transfusion service consults
separately — this lesson names it so you recognize the citation when your Quality Analyst uses
it, not to teach its contents.

And now the reason Tuesday's three components are already running on different clocks, from the
dating table in `sources/cfr/610.53.md`:

| Product | Storage temperature | Dating period |
|---|---|---|
| Red Blood Cells, additive solution | Between 1 and 6 °C | 42 days from date of collection |
| Red Blood Cells, irradiated | Between 1 and 6 °C | 28 days from date of irradiation, or original dating, whichever is shorter |
| Platelets | Between 20 and 24 °C | 5 days from date of collection |
| Fresh Frozen Plasma | −18 °C or colder | 1 year from date of collection |
| Cryoprecipitated AHF | −18 °C or colder | 1 year from date of collection of source blood (or oldest source blood in a pre-storage pool) |

Same Tuesday donation. Same DIN underneath every one of these. Four completely different
expiration clocks, and the platelets are already burning through theirs the fastest — five days,
full stop, no exceptions in the table for a good storage record. That's the concrete answer to
this module's finish line: one donation becomes several products, and "different shelf lives"
isn't a rounding error, it's a 73-fold difference between the shortest dating period here and the
longest.

## ISBT 128, in full

Module 2 gave you one sentence about this: the donation gets a globally standardized identifier
called the Donation Identification Number, or DIN, under a labeling system called ISBT 128. Here's
the rest of it.

**ISBT 128** is an international standard — not an FDA regulation, not an AABB Standard, a fourth
category worth holding distinctly per the regulatory-landscape foundation lesson's framework —
for the terminology, identification, coding, and labeling of blood, cell, tissue, and other
medical products of human origin. Its name comes from Code 128, the barcode symbology the
standard was originally built around (modern implementations also use 2-D data matrix symbols and
RFID tags, which pack more encoded data into less physical space, but the name stuck).

**ICCBBA** — the International Council for Commonality in Blood Banking Automation — is the
global nonprofit organization that develops and manages ISBT 128, describing its own mission as
enhancing patient safety by leading the standard's development and administration. It's a
registration authority in an active sense, not a one-time publisher: it governs the standard's
content on an ongoing basis, including, as this morning's near-miss shows, the product code
tables that define exactly what each code on a label means.

That governance relationship answers a question this lesson's regulation quote left open: who
actually assigns the "unique facility identifier" that 606.121(c)(2) and (c)(13)(A) require? The
regulation doesn't say. In practice, it's ICCBBA, through ISBT 128, that issues and administers
that identifier to every accredited blood and tissue establishment worldwide — a regulation
requiring *something exist*, and an industry standard supplying *the mechanism* that satisfies
it, exactly the relationship the regulatory-landscape-orientation foundation lesson taught you to
expect.

Four data elements, working together on every ISBT 128 label, are what this module's finish line
actually asks you to be able to read:

- **The Donation Identification Number (DIN).** Assigned at the moment of collection — the number
  module 2 already showed you tying the donor, the bag, and the sample tubes together. It's
  globally unique: no other facility, anywhere, in ISBT 128's registry, will ever assign that
  same number to a different donation. That global uniqueness is what makes it possible for a
  hospital receiving a unit from Lakeshore to trust the number the same way it would trust one
  issued by any other ISBT 128 facility on earth, without needing to know anything about
  Lakeshore's internal systems.
- **The product code.** A separate code from the DIN, identifying exactly what the product *is*
  — the component type, plus whatever modifications were applied (leukoreduced, irradiated,
  washed, pooled) and the anticoagulant or additive solution used. This is the piece that drifted
  in this morning's scenario: two units can share an identical DIN-adjacent appearance and still
  carry meaningfully different product codes if one was irradiated and the other wasn't, and the
  code — not the bag's visual appearance — is what a scanning system and a transfusion service
  actually rely on to know the difference.
- **ABO and Rh**, encoded alongside the human-readable designation required by 606.121(c)(9).
- **Expiration date (and hour, where required)**, encoded to match exactly what 606.121(c)(4)(i)
  and the 610.53 dating table require in human-readable form.

Put together, those four elements are why a "globally governed identifier" — really, a whole
governed *system* of identifiers — is the backbone of traceability for this course. A DIN that
means the same thing everywhere, checked against a product code table that means the same thing
everywhere, is what lets Lakeshore, a hospital three states away, and an FDA investigator all
agree on what a bag of blood actually is, without trusting each other's internal records. Break
that agreement silently, with no physical product ever being wrong, and you've still broken the
thing the barcode exists to provide.

This is also where BECS earns its third clause in this course's running definition: system of
record for donor eligibility (module 1), gate for quarantine release (module 2), and here,
**it controls whether a final label can print** — exactly the control this morning's forty units
passed through, using data that had drifted without anyone treating the drift as a change.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reconstructing this morning's forty units doesn't ask
Lakeshore to characterize the incident. They ask for specific artifacts.

**The product code table version history** — proof of exactly when the ICCBBA update was
received, when it was applied inside BECS, and what changed between the old and new versions for
the affected codes. Without this, nobody can answer the threshold question: did the meaning of
these units' printed codes actually change in a way that matters?

**The change record for the vendor's software push itself** — treated as a change to a production
system, under the written procedure 606.100(b) already requires Lakeshore to maintain for its
labeling operations (a citation from the regulatory-landscape-orientation foundation lesson). A
push with no advance review, no test, and no documented risk assessment of what happens to units
mid-print is itself a finding — the same shape of gap the risk-and-controls-vocabulary foundation
lesson called out: a conclusion with the reasoning missing.

**The donor/lot number and DIN record** for each of the forty units, tying each one back to its
donation under the identity link 606.160(c) already established in module 2 — proof that whatever
correction happens next reaches every affected unit, not just the ones someone remembers.

A bad answer to "how do you know which units printed against the outdated table" sounds like "the
supervisor noticed something looked off at shift change." That's a lucky catch, not a control. The
control an inspector expects is a timestamped, queryable record of which print jobs ran against
which table version — the same shape of evidence module 2 taught you to expect for quarantine
status, applied here to label content instead of release status.

## Common traps

**"The label is just a sticker — printing it correctly is a packaging concern, not a quality
concern."** This morning's scenario is built specifically to break that assumption. Nothing about
the physical product changed; the entire problem lives in whether printed, coded data still
matches a governed standard's current definition. 606.121 is a CGMP labeling regulation, not a
packaging spec, precisely because a label that misrepresents what a product is — even subtly,
even only in a barcode nobody but a scanner reads — is exactly as dangerous as a labeling error
someone can see with their own eyes. Arguably more dangerous, because nobody visually double-checks
a machine-readable field the way they'd double-check printed text.

**"ISBT 128 is an FDA requirement."** It's an easy assumption, because 606.121(c)(13) requires a
machine-readable barcode and nearly every U.S. blood establishment uses ISBT 128 to satisfy that
requirement — but read the regulation's own words again: it requires a CBER-approved
machine-readable format containing four specific data elements. It never names ISBT 128. ISBT 128
is industry-standard tier, maintained by ICCBBA, layered on top of a regulation that requires
*something* like it to exist without mandating that specific standard by name. Calling ISBT 128
"the FDA rule" in a deviation report or a vendor conversation is the same category mistake the
regulatory-landscape-orientation foundation lesson opened with, just with a new source at the top
of the sentence.

**"All the components from one donation share the same expiration date, since they came from the
same draw."** They don't, and 610.53's dating table is the proof: platelets from Tuesday's
donation expire in five days; the red cells have 42 if they're in additive solution; the plasma,
frozen, is good for a year. Treating "one donation" as "one expiration date" is a fast way to miss
that the platelets need attention on a completely different timeline than everything else that
same draw produced.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask whether a vendor's "routine data update" to a production labeling system went through the
  same change control as any other production change** — advance review, test run, coordinated
  timing, documented risk assessment. A product code table looks like reference data. It behaves
  like a live configuration change the moment it's wired into a system that prints labels on it.
- **When a labeling deviation lands on your desk, ask whether it's a wrong-physical-product
  problem or a wrong-data-describing-a-correct-product problem before you accept a proposed fix.**
  They look similar in a deviation summary and require completely different corrective actions.
- **Push back on "ISBT 128 requires it" as a stand-alone citation.** Ask whether the actual
  requirement traces to 606.121 (regulation, FDA-enforced) or to the standard layered on top
  (industry-standard tier, ICCBBA-governed). The escalation path and who owns the fix differ.
- **Treat the product code table the way you'd treat any authoritative external reference data
  your systems depend on** — know who owns updating it, how your systems consume new versions,
  and what your rollback plan is if a version turns out to have been applied incorrectly.
- **When "nothing shipped" is the whole story on a labeling near-miss, ask what the actual
  detection margin was** — the same likelihood/severity/detectability discipline from the
  risk-and-controls-vocabulary foundation lesson applies here exactly as it did to the platelet
  label swap in that lesson's own scenario.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: The Quality Analyst reports that the forty units' ABO/Rh, DIN, and expiration dates are all still correct — only the product code is a table-revision behind. Does that mean they're fine to release as-is?

No. 606.121(c)(13)(iii)(C) lists the product code as one of the required minimum elements of the
machine-readable barcode, on equal footing with facility identifier, lot number, and ABO/Rh — it's
not a lesser field. An outdated product code may still describe exactly the right product, or it
may not; the whole point of a governed, centrally revised table is that Lakeshore can't know which
without checking the specific code against the current version. Until that check happens — and,
if needed, the label is corrected — these units aren't release-eligible, even though nothing about
the physical product itself is in question.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: True or false: 21 CFR 606.121 requires blood establishments to label their products using ISBT 128.

False. 606.121(c)(13) requires a machine-readable barcode, approved by CBER, containing a unique
facility identifier, donor/lot number, product code, and ABO/Rh — but the regulation's text never
names ISBT 128. ISBT 128, maintained by ICCBBA, is the near-universal industry standard blood
establishments use to satisfy that requirement, not a standard the regulation itself mandates by
name. That makes it industry-standard tier under the regulatory-landscape-orientation foundation's
four-tier framework — practically universal in the U.S. blood industry, but not itself the source
of the legal requirement.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Tuesday's single donation produced red cells, plasma, and platelets. Since they all came from the same draw and carry the same underlying DIN, do they share one expiration date?

No. 610.53(b)'s dating table sets a separate clock for each product type and storage condition:
platelets stored at room temperature expire in 5 days from collection; red cells in additive
solution get 42 days; frozen plasma is good for a year. Same donation, same DIN tying them
together for traceability — but four (or more) completely different expiration clocks running in
parallel from the moment of separation. The platelets are always the most time-pressured product
of the group, regardless of how the rest of the donation is doing.
:::

## Where this goes next

However this morning's forty units get resolved, the pattern this module teaches doesn't change:
a component isn't release-eligible until it carries a complete, correct label — human-readable
content matching 606.121, a machine-readable barcode whose every element, including the product
code, checks out against the current standard, and an expiration clock specific to exactly what
it is. Module 4, `storage-distribution-and-hemovigilance`, picks up from a component that's
cleared that bar: how a released, correctly labeled unit is stored and monitored, shipped, handed
off to a hospital's own transfusion service, and — if something still goes wrong after all of
this — what has to happen and be reported next.
